## Introduction

**Background & Motivation:**

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is currently the principal cause of death in the United States, with an American dying of heart disease every 34 seconds [@birger2021spending] [@cdc_heart_disease_facts_2024]. The disease develops through a combination of biological, behavioral, and lifestyle factors that accumulate over time, and while certain communities experience higher risk, heart disease dominates across race and gender lines. Not only a pressing public health issue, CVD poses an immense financial burden on the United States, accounting for over $320 billion in annual spending across the board for insurance cost, health care treatment of hypertension, service price, etc [@birger2021spending]. As such, understanding the factors that contribute to heart disease is of critical public health concern in terms of identifying which communities deserve most medical intervention and where preventative efforts should be aimed. Utilizing a 2022 data set on the indicators of heart disease, this study investigates how demographic factors (e.g. sex, age, race) and health factors (e.g. smoking, drinking, previous health conditions, sleep) impact the probability that an individual will experience a heart attack.

We hypothesized that previous health complications (e.g. diabetes, kidney disease) would increase the probability of heart attack. Likewise, we expected that increased sleep would lower heart disease risk due to the benefits of sleep on general health and physical recovery. Using White individuals as a baseline, we furthermore predicted that Black, Native American, and Hispanic individuals may be at higher risk for heart attack due to historic disenfranchisement that has impacted access to education, food sources, health care, etc – limitations which would likely negatively impact these communities’ health outcomes, including cardiovascular health. 

In addition to studying heart disease risk, we investigated the factors that influence body mass index (BMI). Calculated from an individual's height and weight, BMI is commonly used in research and healthcare as a simple measure of obesity (one of the most widely studied contributors to CVD) and as a proxy for cardiometabolic health. Obesity is closely tied to factors such as physical activity, smoking, and other lifestyle habits [@powell2021obesity]. Therefore, understanding its role in cardiovascular health requires considering it within this broader network of influences. Higher BMI is generally associated with higher probability of cardiovascular conditions, including heart disease and failure [@carbone2022impact]. However, this relationship is not uniform across populations. Research on the "obesity paradox" suggests that in certain contexts BMI does not always align with expected health outcomes [@tutor2023updates]. As a result, BMI is best understood as an accessible but imperfect indicator that reflects multiple underlying influences.

Because of this, BMI is most informative when examined alongside behavioral and demographic factors that affect cardiovascular health. Smoking, physical activity, and self-reported health status are all associated with CVD outcomes and help explain differences in BMI across individuals [@powell2021obesity]. These behaviors also tend to co-occur, forming broader patterns of health behavior that influence both weight and long-term disease risk. Accordingly, this study asks how BMI is associated with these behavioral and demographic characteristics. Based on prior studies, we predicted BMI to be higher among individuals who report lower physical activity, poorer general health, and smoking behavior. We also expected BMI to vary across demographic characteristics, particularly age, reflecting differences in lifestyle patterns and accumulated health risks over time.
